claims.text: The as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloy has an ordered single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited alloy has a limited surface-to-volume ratio.
Nanoscale grain-boundary density and distribution predominantly govern the alloy's low-field magnetocaloric response and hysteresis.
Nanoscale grain boundaries act as pinning centers for magnetic domain-wall motion.
The grain-boundary distribution modulates internal strain fields.
Rapid thermal annealing can refine the grains and thereby increase nanoscale grain-boundary density in this alloy.
Rapid thermal annealing can modify the structure and magnetic properties of magnetic alloy films.
A moderate-temperature, short-duration RTA can increase grain-boundary formation without inducing phase separation.
The proposed RTA can preserve overall composition and mechanical stability.
The proposed RTA can maintain rapid heat-exchange capability.
Increasing grain-boundary density reduces domain-wall pinning effects.
Increasing grain-boundary density promotes a broader and more gradual magnetostructural transition.
Broadening the magnetostructural transition reduces magnetocaloric hysteresis.
The RTA-treated alloy will retain a significant magnetocaloric entropy change.
Relative to the as-deposited alloy, the RTA-treated alloy will have a broader, less abrupt magnetocaloric transition.
Relative to the as-deposited alloy, the RTA-treated alloy will exhibit reduced hysteretic loss during low-field cooling cycles.
The RTA treatment will leave the transition temperature comparable to the baseline or shift it only modestly.
The as-deposited baseline exhibits a sharp, hysteretic first-order magnetostructural transition.
Low applied fields below 1 T are a regime in which magnetic irreversibility can be observed in compositionally complex alloys.
The predictions are limited to processing conditions that avoid secondary phases and significant compositional segregation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls grain boundaries pinning centers, whereas the mechanism says increasing their density reduces domain-wall pinning. No additional distinction in boundary type, spacing, or strain state is supplied to reconcile these opposite effects.

The initial state is described as having a limited surface-to-volume ratio, yet the RTA is said to maintain rapid heat exchange even though the intervention does not alter sample geometry or otherwise explain how that limitation is removed.
